list.listitem: Hordeolum (stye) is an acute, tender, and erythematous lesion of the eyelid that can safely be treated with warm compresses and topical erythromycin. C
Chalazia usually present as a chronic, nontender, subcutaneous nodule within the eyelid, sometimes interfering with complete opening of the eyelid. C
Lesions failing conservative treatment should be incised and drained. C
Sebaceous carcinoma should be suspected in patients who are middle-aged and older with persistent chalazia. C

background.definition: Hordeolum is an acute, erythematous, and tender lump within the eyelid, commonly referred to as a stye. Chalazion is a chronic subcutaneous nodule within the eyelid.

list.listitem: The exact incidence for this very common condition is unknown.
Most commonly, hordeolum is caused by Staphylococcal bacteria. MRSA infection is a rare but possible cause.
Patients with chronic blepharitis, seborrheic dermatitis, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and acne rosacea are at increased risk for developing chalazia.
A hordeolum is an acute infection of the Meibomian gland (internal) or the glands of Zeiss or Moll (external).

A chalazion results from obstruction of the Meibomian gland duct, causing release of the gland's contents into the surrounding soft tissue of the eyelid. This incites a lipogranulomatous reaction. Occasionally, these may become secondarily infected.
An acute, tender, and erythematous lesion of the eyelid is clinically consistent with hordeola. C
Chalazia usually present as a chronic, nontender, subcutaneous nodule within the eyelid, sometimes interfering with complete opening of the eyelid. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Well-demarcated, flat or elevated, and pigmented or nonpigmented
Hyperpigmented, hyperkeratotic lesion with a stuck-on appearance
Translucent cyst at the lid margin
Occurs in middle-aged to elderly patients and can mimic chalazia

list.listitem: An acute, tender, and erythematous lesion of the eyelid is clinically consistent with hordeola.
Chalazia usually presents as a chronic, nontender, SC nodule within the eyelid, sometimes interfering with complete opening of the eyelid.

In the vast majority of cases, the diagnosis can be made based on the clinical picture. However, clinical diagnosis of periocular lesions is less than optimal for both primary care clinicians and ophthalmologists.
Although Staphylococcus aureus is commonly associated with hordeola, routine culture is unnecessary as cultures do not correlate with clinical improvement.
Fine-needle aspiration may be used to distinguish benign eyelid lesions from malignant ones.

Chalazia and hordeola are diagnosed clinically. Chalazia are typically chronic lesions; hordeola are typically acute lesions. Lesions clinically diagnosed as hordeola, histologically may be chalazia. Fortunately, the treatment is the same for both.
When uncertain of the diagnosis or there is concern for malignancy, persistent lesions should be biopsied.
Initial treatment includes warm compresses 4 times daily and topical erythromycin ointment. C
Lesions refractory to treatment should be referred for incision and drainage. C
Intralesional triamcinolone may be an effective alternative to incision and drainage. C

Hordeola are most commonly treated with warm compresses. Topical erythromycin ointment may be used, especially if there is associated blepharitis or persistent inflammation, though evidence from placebo-controlled trials is lacking. Oral antibiotics such as cephalexin or dicloxacillin may be considered for more severe cases, particularly those with preseptal cellulitis or multiple lesions. Topical aminoglycosides are generally not first-line due to limited evidence of benefit. No randomized, placebo-controlled trials have definitively established the efficacy of these treatments.
Although rare, hordeola can be caused caused by Methicillin resistant S. aureus which can be considered if first line treatments fail.
Chalazion may be injected with corticosteroids; typically 1 to 2 treatments are sufficient.

Treatment with antibiotic is not likely to improve the resolution of a chalazion or hordeolum. In a retrospective review (n=2,712), the addition of an antibiotic to conservative measures for a chalazion (adjusted RR, 0.97, 95% CI, 0.89-1.04, P=0.393) or hordeolum (adjusted RR, 0.99, 95% CI, 0.96-1.02, P=0.489) was not associated with an increased likelihood of treatment success.
In children, initial treatment with topical antibiotic or steroid drops did not reduce the need for surgical intervention (incision or steroid injection) compared to warm compresses alone. ​

Eyelid hygiene speeds chalazion resolution: A randomized trial of 50 adults with chalazia showed that adding microblepharoexfoliation (MBE), an in-office eyelid margin cleaning procedure, to standard lid hygiene significantly increased 1-month lesion resolution (87% resolved vs 44% with standard care).
Hordeola that do not respond to conservative measures after 1 to 2 weeks should be referred for excision and drainage.
Incision and curettage is the treatment of choice for chalazia in patients 35 years and older and for chalazia that are present for more than 8 months or larger than 11.4 mm.

New evidence supports intense pulsed light therapy with meibomian gland expression (IPL-MGX) as an effective alternative to incision & curettage for chalazia. In a 2023 study (95 lesions per group), IPL-MGX achieved a similar resolution rate (~70% at 1 month) to surgery, while significantly reducing recurrence and improving tear film stability.
Warm compresses may provide symptomatic relief and hasten resolution.

Accupuncture and bloodletting as an adjunctive therapy to eye drops may improve symptoms for hordeolum. However, the trials were small and had bias, so higher-quality studies are needed before routine use.

A small RCT in adults with chalaziosis (eyelid chalazia) reported that adding an oral probiotic supplement to standard warm compress and antibiotic/steroid ointment therapy shortened the healing time for small chalazia (on average ~21 days vs ~39 days)​. There was no benefit for larger lesions, but this finding raises interest in a possible gut microbiome influence on eyelid gland inflammation.
Hordeolum that fail treatment should be referred for incision and drainage.
Chalazion that persist beyond 4 weeks, or recur, should be referred for excision given the potential for malignancy.
Most hordeola resolve with conservative treatment within 4 to 7 days. C
